title: What an argument for God is
note: An argument for God gives premises meant to support the conclusion that God exists. Deductive arguments aim to guarantee it; inductive and abductive ones aim to make it probable or the best explanation; a cumulative case weighs many lines of evidence together. Most target the God of classical theism: one necessary, all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good creator.

read.title: What a theistic argument must do
text: An argument for God, like any argument, is a set of premises offered in support of a conclusion. A deductive argument aims at validity: if its premises are true, its conclusion cannot be false. A simple template runs:
(1) If the universe depends on something beyond itself, a being beyond nature exists. (2) The universe depends on something beyond itself. (3) Therefore, a being beyond nature exists.

The work lies in defending premise (2). Other arguments are inductive or abductive: they claim that God's existence makes the evidence more probable, or explains it better, than any rival hypothesis does. Richard Swinburne calls an argument C-inductive if it merely raises the probability of its conclusion, and P-inductive if it makes the conclusion more probable than not.

A standard objection, pressed by Hume and Kant, is the gap problem: even a sound argument for a first cause or a designer reaches only that cause or designer, not the one, all-powerful, perfectly good God of theism.

Theists reply in two ways. Some, like Aquinas, argue from what the first cause must be to further attributes, such as simplicity and perfection. Others, like Basil Mitchell and Swinburne, treat the arguments as a cumulative case, in which each argument supplies part of the picture and the whole is stronger than any single part.
